newsitem.title: USA: SEC CHAIRMAN'S TRAVEL PRACTICES SCRUTINIZED - POST.
newsitem.headline: SEC CHAIRMAN'S TRAVEL PRACTICES SCRUTINIZED - POST.

text.p: U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission Chairman Arthur Levitt used government-paid upgrades and reimbursements to help reduce his own costs when choosing more expensive accommodations than government travel rules allowed, the Washington Post reported Thursday.

The newspaper, quoting SEC travel documents and other records, said Levitt often flew first class and stayed at luxury hotels, partly at government expense, and sometimes attached personal travel to official trips.
Levitt, the chief regulator of U.S. financial markets, broke no laws, according to the staff of a House subcommittee investigating Levitt's travel expenses.
But they did conclude he "loosely" followed regulations intended to limit government employees from using taxpayer money for first-class air travel or luxury hotel stays, the newspaper said.

"It's clear to me that the SEC loosely applied its own travel policies and the federal travel regulations, particularly in regard to approving first-class travel and other upgrades for Mr. Levitt," the newspaper quoted Representative David McIntosh, a Republican from Indiana, as saying.
McIntosh heads the House Subcommittee on National Economic Growth, Natural Resources and Regulatory Affairs, which has been looking into Levitt's travel practices.
Levitt and his staff told the newspaper there were no improprieties and that he paid for upgrades not permitted by the regulations.

The agency, in letters to the committee, said Levitt violated no government regulations or SEC rules, did not attempt to subsidise his personal travel at the expense of the government, and did not arrange official travel to suit his personal convenience.
The Post said Levitt took 153 offical trips in 175 weeks between September 1993 and November 1996 at a cost of about $110,000, quoting documents obtained under the Freedom of Information Act.
Ninety of those trips were to New York City and 37 included a weekend at Levitt's beachside house in Westport, Conn., or his apartment in New York at his own expense, the Post said.
Levitt also attached eight personal trips to his Santa Fe, New Mexico vacation house to 22 official swings he took to the West Coast and Southwest, the newspaper said.

Federal rules restrict travel arrangements of government employees, and ban first-class travel at government expense except when economy class is not available, when an employee is disabled or when security considerations require it.
